question_text: A colleague's work is not good enough and it is starting to affect the team. Nobody has told them. What do you do?
option_a: Tell them directly, and be specific about what has to change.
option_b: Hint at it gently and hope they pick it up.
option_c: Raise it with their manager rather than with them.
option_d: Say nothing — managing them is not your job.

question_text: You are reviewing a peer's document and it is well below the standard expected. What do you do?
option_a: Leave a general 'looks fine' and move on.
option_b: Pass your concerns to whoever owns the review process.
option_c: Write clear comments on exactly what has to change.
option_d: Note a couple of small points and leave the bigger problem alone.

question_text: A supplier missed their date, so your delivery will be late. Your manager asks why. What do you say?
option_a: That the date has slipped, and what you are doing about it.
option_b: That the supplier failed and it was out of your hands.
option_c: That you should have had a fallback, and you are building one.
option_d: As little as possible until you see where the blame lands.

question_text: A tool you depend on was down all day and you missed your commitment. You are asked what happened. What do you say?
option_a: Nothing specific until you see how it is being taken.
option_b: That the outage had nothing to do with you.
option_c: That you missed it, and what you have already set in motion.
option_d: That you had no contingency, and describe the one you are adding.

question_text: A decision is needed and half the information is missing. Which would you rather do?
option_a: Decide now on what you have and adjust later.
option_b: Wait until the missing information arrives.

question_text: The team is stuck waiting on a figure that may not arrive this week. Which would you rather do?
option_a: Hold the decision until the figure lands.
option_b: Pick a direction now and revisit it when the figure arrives.

question_text: You are already at capacity when you are handed another piece of work. What do you do?
option_a: Say yes and absorb it somehow.
option_b: Say what would have to slip, and ask them to choose.
option_c: Take it, and let something quietly slide.
option_d: Say you cannot take it on.

question_text: Your week is already full when a second manager asks you to pick something up as well. What do you do?
option_a: Accept, and drop whichever task is least visible.
option_b: Set out the trade-off and let the two of them settle the priority.
option_d: Agree, and find the hours somewhere.

question_text: Skipping a required sign-off would let you hit the deadline, and nobody would know. What do you do?
option_a: Skip it — the deadline matters more.
option_b: Get the sign-off and miss the deadline.
option_c: Ask for an exception, on the record.
option_d: Skip it now and have it signed retrospectively.

question_text: A required test suite takes two hours you do not have before release. What do you do?
option_a: Release now and run the suite afterwards.
option_b: Ask openly for permission to release without it.
option_c: Leave it out — it will almost certainly be fine.

question_text: Two people on your team have stopped speaking to each other and it is slowing the work down. What do you do?
option_a: Get them in a room and work it through.
option_b: Talk to each of them separately first.
option_c: Route around them and keep the work moving.
option_d: Stay out of it — they are adults.

question_text: A disagreement between two colleagues is being fought out over email, with you copied in. What do you do?
option_a: Nothing — it is not your argument.
option_b: Reply suggesting the three of you talk it through live.
option_c: Take the parts you need offline and get on with your work.
option_d: Call each of them and hear them out one at a time.
